text.p: Israeli soldiers left their hilltop base in Hebron at dawn on Friday, transferring most of the city to Palestinian rule after 30 years of occupation.
A convoy of jeeps slipped out of the fortress-like military governor's heaquarters overlooking the town and about 100 PLO police officers moved in to the sound of sirens and firecrackers.
Only a small crowd was on hand to witness the handshake between officers that set the long-delayed Israeli redeployment from 80 percent of Hebron in motion.

"We are now carrying out the handover of responsibility on a large portion of the city of Hebron to the Palestinian Authority," local Israeli commander Brigadier-General Gadi said after shaking hands with Palestinian officers.

"We completed the handover in an orderly way...The Palestinian police will take responsibility in a large portion of the city of Hebron," he said, adding that the pullback would be completed before the onset of the Jewish sabbath at sundown.
A lone Palestinian climbed a tall antenna atop the headquarters to raise the Palestinian flag over the building which President Yasser Arafat was expected to visit within a few days.
Few Hebron residents braved the pre-dawn chill to view the handover, the last of seven West Bank transfers under an interim self-rule agreement between Israel and the PLO.
Palestinian Colonel Awni al-Natshe, deputy Hebron commander, said: "Today we will make the life in the city normal."
Crowds had gathered on Thursday night, believing the transfer would take place immediately after the Israeli parliament overwhelmingly approved the deal.
"I am so happy to see them leave. This will give a chance for peace," said Ziad Abu Rajab, an employee of the Hebron municipality watching the handover.
"But my joy is incomplete. They will still be in the downtown area," he said.
Israel will retain about one fifth of the city where some 400 militant Jewish settlers live.
Israel poured troop and police reinforcments into the town to prevent protests by Jewish settlers opposed to the handover.

An Israeli general issued orders on Thursday restricting the movements of 18 alleged Jewish militants for up to 10 days. Some came from Hebron where the settlers live in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs. This makes Hebron unique among the seven West Bank towns already handed over to PLO rule.
Five soldiers for each settler will remain to guard the Jews in the fifth of the town that will remain under Israeli control.
"We are not leaving Hebron, we are redeploying in Hebron," Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said.
His remarks were aimed at right-wingers and settlers who staged a cabinet revolt against the withdrawal.
In Jerusalem, Israel's parliament paved the way for the pullback by endorsing the agreement.
The house voted 87-17, with one abstention, to approve the Hebron deal and three further troop redeployments from mainly rural areas of the West Bank.
The accord, clinched after months of acrimonious negotiations, marked the first time a right-wing government had agreed to hand over territory Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East war to PLO rule.
The main opposition Labour party and left-wing and Arab factions joined with most members of the ruling Likud coalition to ratify the accord after a 12-hour debate.

"I thank the members of the house. I hope in the future, during this government's term, to bring complete peace agreements with the Palestinians and perhaps with Arab nations, in addition to the ones we have signed," Netanyahu told parliament.
Brigadier-General Gadi, as the last Israeli to leave the headquarters, was asked to say something important to mark the historic occasion. "History speaks for itself," he said.
